summary: After Herod dies, God brings Jesus out of Egypt and guides Joseph away from Judea to Nazareth in Galilee, where the Child grows in wisdom and grace.
key_insight: In Matthew, Joseph is directed by God in a dream four times (1:20; 2:13; 2:19; 2:22), and each time he simply gets up and does what he is told. Matthew never records a single word from him.
story: After Herod died, an angel of the Lord appeared in a dream to Joseph in Egypt: “Arise, take the young Child and His mother, and go to the land of Israel, for those who sought the young Child’s life are dead.” So Joseph got up, took the young Child and His mother, and came into the land of Israel. {Mt}
But he heard that Archelaus was reigning over Judea in place of his father Herod, and he was afraid to go there. Warned by God in a dream, he turned aside into the region of Galilee. {Mt}

So the family came back to Nazareth in Galilee, their own city, {Lk} and Joseph settled there. Matthew saw in this the fulfillment of what was spoken by the prophets: “He shall be called a Nazarene.” {Mt}
There the Child grew and became strong in spirit, filled with wisdom; and the grace of God was upon Him. {Lk}
differences: Matthew tells of two dreams, Joseph’s fear of Archelaus and the turn to Galilee. Luke says only that they returned to Galilee, to their own city, Nazareth.
Luke places the return right after Jesus’ presentation in the temple, “when they had performed all things according to the law of the Lord.” He does not mention the wise men or Egypt.
Matthew links the move to Scripture: “He shall be called a Nazarene.” Luke calls Nazareth “their own city” and adds a summary of the Child’s growth.

fit.question: Luke says that after the presentation in the temple, Joseph and Mary returned to Nazareth. Matthew tells of the wise men in Bethlehem and a flight to Egypt, and only then a move to Nazareth, which Joseph seems to choose after hearing about Archelaus. How do the two fit?

points.label: Luke passes over a stretch of time
points.text: Luke moves from the temple to Nazareth in one sentence and does not mention the months in Bethlehem and Egypt. Ancient writers often did this. Luke does the same in Acts, where Paul’s time in Arabia and Damascus (Galatians 1:17–18) is covered by the words “after many days” (Acts 9:23). Bethlehem is only about six miles from the temple, so the family could easily have gone back there after the presentation.

points.label: Nazareth was home all along
points.text: Luke shows that Joseph and Mary lived in Nazareth before the birth (Luke 1:26–27; 2:4). Matthew never says they lived in Bethlehem first; he simply begins his story there. Joseph seems to have planned to settle in Judea, perhaps in David’s town, and the dream sent him back to the home Luke describes.

fit.note: Each writer tells a true part of the story, and neither says anything the other denies.
fit.short: Luke passes over the months in Bethlehem and Egypt; Matthew tells them, and explains why the family went home to Nazareth rather than Judea.

scene.label: Archelaus
scene.text: When Herod died, Rome divided his kingdom among his sons. Archelaus received Judea, Samaria and Idumea and soon proved as violent as his father; Josephus says he had about three thousand people killed at one Passover early in his reign. Rome removed him in AD 6.

scene.label: Galilee under Antipas
scene.text: Galilee went to another son, Herod Antipas, who ruled it for more than forty years. This is the Herod who later beheaded John the Baptist and whom Jesus called “that fox” (Luke 13:32).

scene.label: Nazareth
scene.text: Nazareth was a small village in the hills of lower Galilee, never mentioned in the Old Testament. People from elsewhere thought little of it: “Can anything good come out of Nazareth?” (John 1:46). The rebuilt city of Sepphoris stood about four miles away.

scene.label: “A Nazarene”
scene.text: No single Old Testament verse says these words, and Matthew says “the prophets,” plural. The name Nazareth sounds like the Hebrew netzer, “branch,” the word Isaiah uses for the Messiah: “a Branch shall grow out of his roots” (Isaiah 11:1). “Nazarene” also became a term of contempt (Acts 24:5), fitting the prophets’ picture of a Messiah “despised and rejected by men” (Isaiah 53:3).

witnesses.matthew: Explains how the Son of David, born in Bethlehem, came to be known as Jesus of Nazareth. Matthew shows God guiding every step by dreams and Scripture, so that even an out-of-the-way village becomes part of the plan.
witnesses.luke: Gives no travel story, only a family that kept the law and a Child who grew. Luke’s summary echoes what he wrote of John the Baptist (Luke 1:80), and he returns to it after the temple visit (2:52), showing the Son of God growing up as a real boy.

seeing.reveals: The Son of God spent His childhood in an obscure village, growing in body and spirit like any child, with the grace of God upon Him.
seeing.living: Most of Jesus’ life on earth was spent in Nazareth, in years the Gospels pass over in a sentence. God’s grace was at work in those years too. The quiet seasons of growing, working and waiting are not outside His purpose.
seeing.ponder: What would change if you believed that God is at work in your own hidden years, the ones no one else notices?

preaching.big_idea: God led His Son home through quiet obedience to a town the world despised.
outline: God works through a despised place (23)
preaching.watch_for: The angel’s words in verse 20 echo God’s word to Moses: “all the men who sought your life are dead” (Exodus 4:19). Like Moses, the Child returns to His people when the danger has passed.
